nameStory: The Bent-lined Carpet gets its name from the distinctive zigzag or bent line that runs across its wings, creating a pattern reminiscent of an old-fashioned carpet design. Many geometer moths are called "carpets" because their intricate wing patterns resemble the geometric designs found in woven rugs and tapestries.
description: The Bent-lined Carpet is a small, delicate moth with intricate geometric wing patterns typical of the geometer family. Its wings span just 17-23 millimeters (about the size of a nickel), making it one of the smaller moths you'll encounter. The wings display beautiful earth-toned patterns with the characteristic bent or zigzag lines that give this species its name. Like other geometer moths, it holds its wings horizontally when at rest, creating a triangular silhouette.

idTips.label: Bent wing line
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive zigzag or bent line running across both forewings - this crooked line is usually darker than the surrounding wing color and creates sharp angles rather than smooth curves

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small wingspan of 17-23mm makes it about nickel-sized when wings are spread - noticeably smaller than many other moths you'll see at lights

idTips.label: Wing position
idTips.description: Rests with wings held horizontally outward from the body, creating a flat, triangular profile rather than tent-like or folded back

idTips.label: Earth-toned coloration
idTips.description: Wings display muted browns, grays, and tans with subtle geometric patterns that help it blend with tree bark when resting during the day

idTips.label: Body build
idTips.description: Slender body typical of geometer moths, much thinner than the robust, fuzzy bodies of sphinx or giant silk moths

habitat: Look for Bent-lined Carpets in areas where knotweed and smartweed plants grow, as their caterpillars depend on these Polygonum species for food. You'll find them in disturbed areas like roadsides, vacant lots, field edges, and gardens where these weedy plants thrive. They're attracted to porch lights and outdoor lighting from suburban areas to rural farmland throughout New England.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin appearing in May, often seen at porch lights and outdoor lighting during warm evenings. This is when the first generation of the year emerges from overwintering pupae.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with multiple overlapping generations - you're most likely to spot them at lights during June through August. Caterpillars are actively feeding on knotweed plants during this time.
seasonality.fall: Adults continue flying through September and October, with the final generation preparing to overwinter. Look for them at lights during warm autumn nights.
seasonality.winter: No adult activity - they spend winter as pupae in the soil or leaf litter, waiting for spring warmth to trigger emergence.

funFact: This tiny New England native has become a world traveler - it has somehow managed to establish populations across the Atlantic in Great Britain and even reached remote Atlantic islands like the Azores and Madeira, likely hitchhiking on ships or cargo despite being less than an inch across!
confusionNotes: The Bent-lined Carpet can be confused with other small geometer moths, but the distinctive bent or zigzag line across the forewings is your best identifier - most other carpet moths have straighter lines, wavy lines, or completely different patterns without those sharp angular bends.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its common name suggesting it travels frequently, the "traveller" nickname likely refers to its habit of being attracted to lights and appearing in unexpected places rather than any actual migratory behavior - it's the accidental human-assisted travel that has made it a true globetrotter.
compareHints: The Bent-lined Carpet is the only species in its genus Costaconvexa found in New England, making it unique among our local geometer moths. Compared to other carpet moths in the region, it's distinguished by its smaller size and the characteristic sharp, angular bent line across the forewings rather than the smoother curved or straight lines found on related species.
